summary.text: The Southern Oscillation is the atmospheric side of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, a seesaw in surface air pressure between the tropical eastern and western Pacific.
It is coupled with changes in Pacific sea surface temperature, and wind, surface air pressure and cloudiness all respond to it.
Its negative phase, during El Niño, brings abnormally high pressure over Indonesia and low pressure over the East Pacific, and its positive phase during La Niña is the reverse.

paragraphs.heading: The atmosphere's half
paragraphs.text: The Southern Oscillation is a seesaw in surface air pressure between the tropical eastern Pacific and the tropical western Pacific. It is the atmospheric partner of a swing in ocean temperature, and the two are locked together. The pair makes up the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, or ENSO, a worldwide climate pattern seen as rising and falling sea surface temperatures across the tropical Pacific. Wind, cloud cover and surface air pressure all shift as the oscillation swings.

paragraphs.heading: Two sides of the seesaw
paragraphs.text: The oscillation has a negative phase and a positive phase. In the negative phase, which comes with El Niño, air pressure is unusually high over Indonesia and the western Pacific and unusually low over the eastern Pacific. In the positive phase, which comes with La Niña, the pattern is reversed. Today the name El Niño refers to the warm and negative phase of ENSO. The system flips between El Niño, La Niña and neutral conditions irregularly, roughly every two to seven years, with each event differing in strength.

paragraphs.heading: The usual state of the Pacific
paragraphs.text: In the background, strong trade winds near the equator drive surface water out of the eastern Pacific and into the western Pacific. The push of the wind on the sea is balanced by a slope in the sea surface itself. As a result, sea level near Indonesia is usually about 0.5 m higher than near Peru. The eastern tropical Pacific is also, on average, roughly 8–10 °C cooler at the surface than the west.

paragraphs.heading: How air and sea feed each other
paragraphs.text: A central mechanism of ENSO is the Bjerknes feedback, named for Jacob Bjerknes in 1969. Changes in the atmosphere alter sea temperatures, and the new sea temperatures change the winds in turn, so each reinforces the other. Weaker easterly trade winds let warm surface water surge east and reduce upwelling, the rise of cooler deep water, along the equator. That warms the sea surface, which is El Niño, and weakens the Walker circulation, an east–west loop of overturning air, which weakens the trade winds further. Eventually the warm water in the western tropical Pacific runs down enough for conditions to return to normal, though the exact causes are still being studied.

paragraphs.heading: Reach across the globe
paragraphs.text: ENSO shapes the climate of much of the tropics and subtropics. It also has teleconnections, meaning links to regions at higher latitudes. Its strength tends to peak during the northern hemisphere winter, while regional effects may peak at other times. It is hard to predict, but many weather organisations monitor it closely. The countries hit hardest are developing nations on the Pacific that depend on farming and fishing.
